articles.summary: Thomas Markle, the estranged 82-year-old father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was sent back to jail in Florida on Tuesday after removing his
articles.body: Thomas Markle, the estranged 82-year-old father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was sent back to jail in Florida on Tuesday after removing his court-ordered electronic ankle monitor. The move violated the conditions of his pre-trial release, just days after he was arrested and charged with possessing child sexual abuse material.A US magistrate judge ordered him to remain in federal custody without bond.Thomas Markle was arrested on Friday in Lakeland, Florida, and appeared before a federal court in Tampa after authorities discovered that he had cut off his ankle monitor at around 1.45 am on Monday. First assistant US attorney Bill Essayli said the authorities had sought to revoke his release following the violation.“Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions,” Essayli said.US magistrate judge Lindsay Griffin agreed that Markle should be taken back into custody. In her written order, she noted that his “housing situation” had become “untenable”, but did not elaborate further.Markle had been staying at a senior care facility in Lakeland. His defence attorney, Mary Claire Wolf, had sought to keep him out of custody but had not been able to find a suitable alternative place for him to stay, according to a hearing summary.Essayli told The Associated Press that he did not know why Markle had removed the monitoring device. It was also unclear where the incident took place. Wolf did not immediately respond to requests for comment.Charges against Thomas MarkleThomas Markle was arrested on Friday and charged with a single federal count of possessing child sexual abuse material. The charges followed the seizure of around 78 items from two storage units in the Los Angeles area that he had rented since 2008.The seized material included photographic slides, film negatives and books containing suspected images of child sexual abuse, Essayli said.According to an FBI affidavit filed in court, the material included two explicit photographs of Markle posing with a naked underage girl, along with other images showing children in various stages of undress.One of the photographs reportedly showed a naked girl in a room that appeared to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines, where Markle had previously lived. The couple have two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet.Meghan recently said she was “deeply distressed” by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her father's former home in the Philippines.She also disclosed that a letter containing “troubling allegations” about him had been sent to police in London in 2019. Meghan said she had been assured that the allegations were being investigated.“It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated,” Meghan said of the letter.“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them.”Thomas Markle's health and legal proceedingsThomas Markle had been living in the Philippines before suffering a stroke earlier this year. articles.title: Six things to know about Queen Mary 2
articles.summary: The Southampton-based liner is celebrating its 450th transatlantic crossing.
articles.body:
The only remaining transatlantic liner, Queen Mary 2, has reached a milestone with its 450th crossing.

The record-breaking vessel left Southampton on Tuesday on the seven-day voyage to New York.

The Cunard flagship is an echo of the golden age of transatlantic liners from the early part of the 20th Century.

But how much do you know about its history?

Queen Mary 2 still holds records for being the longest, widest and tallest ocean liner ever built.

Designer Stephen Payne previously said its 345m (1,132ft) length was the most he could fit into Southampton Port's turning basin and at the New York piers.

It was also designed to fit just under New York's Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, with a minimum headroom of 2.7m (9ft).

As a result, Queen Mary 2 has a shortened funnel, reaching a height above the waterline of nearly 62m (203ft).

When it entered service in 2004, it was also the longest and heaviest passenger ship in general, although those records have since been broken.

Payne said he convinced Cunard to create a purpose-built liner, not a cruise ship.

Queen Mary 2 is designed for long ocean crossings rather than port-hopping.

It has a thicker hull, a structural form fit for transatlantic storms and greater power and stability.

However, Payne said those choices meant less room for cabins and a need for extra steel.

That generated a 40% overall extra cost, he recalled.

Queen Mary 2 may be considered by some to be a British icon, but it is truly international.

The ship was officially named by Queen Elizabeth II after her grandmother, who was consort to King George V.

Based in Southampton, it follows in the wake of the QE2 and Queen Mary, both icons of British maritime tradition.

"Land of Hope of Glory" was sung at the ship's keel-laying ceremony in 2002.

However, construction took place at the St Nazaire shipyard near Nantes, France, and it was a French choir and orchestra who performed the patriotic Elgar song.

Cunard, a subsidiary of US cruise firm Carnival, paid an initial $800m for the ship, with millions more spent on subsequent refurbishing.

The liner frequently makes world voyages and its crew comes from more than 50 countries.

According to Payne, part of the ship's design was inspired by boyhood memories of Bournemouth beach.

He has said the front face of the upper decks is like a sandcastle, whose front has been washed away by the sea, leaving a conical shape.

BBC TV's Blue Peter also has a famous role in the ship's story.

When he was seven, Payne watched a report in which presenter Valerie Singleton said there would never be another big liner.

Payne wrote to the programme to tell them they were wrong and promised he would one day design one himself.

The editor replied with a Blue Peter badge and advised him not to be too disappointed if it never happened.

Is 450 transatlantic crossings a record?

Queen Mary's 1,001 crossings between 1936 and 1967 are the most for a passenger liner. They include its service as a troop-ship during World War Two.

Another liner, QE2, made more than 800 crossings between 1969 and 2008.

Turnaround times in port have become faster over the years.

Queen Mary 2 is in and out of port the same day, often within 12 hours, while QE2's stops lasted for two or three days in its early years.

The liner's 2,600-or-more guests have a wide variety of entertainment and dining options.

It boasts the largest sprung dance floor at sea as well as the biggest ocean-going library, with more than 8,500 books.

Other entertainments include a nightclub, casino, theatre, cinema, five-a-side football, fencing classes and four swimming pools.

A dozen restaurants cater for a range of tastes and cabin classes.

The ship also claims to have the only ocean-going kennels, for passengers travelling with pets.

articles.title: North Ockenden: 'Do we need the largest data centre in Europe here?'
articles.summary: Green belt land in North Ockenden is the proposed site for a huge data centre campus, one of the largest in Europe.
articles.body:
North Ockendon in Havering, east London, is right in the middle of London's green belt on the edge of the capital. But it might not be green belt for much longer if developers have their way.

These fields are the proposed site for a huge data centre campus - one of the largest in Europe.

Developers Digital Reef say it would create jobs and be the most sustainable in the world, but the locals don't want it and say it would destroy their lives.

And this development shows the dilemma and many of the issues around data centres. They are necessary for much of modern life. But where do you put them and at what cost?

Danny Leach, who lives locally, says his property "is going to be like a bull's eye on a dartboard" if the plans get the go-ahead.

"There will be the construction for the next eight to 20 years. There will be noise, there's going to be another thousand vehicles a day they're saying," he says.

"There will be disruption, the mess, and then, obviously, when it's operational, the background noise the data centres make and the amount of electric it uses - we already have two power cuts a month here.

"We all need data, but do we need the largest data centre in Europe in this location?"

Graham Ford is also against the proposed development.

"This is rural. This is country. Leave it as it is," he says.

Emma Edmonds adds: "Most people absolutely don't want this.

"It's sacrilege to just build something like that here. It's not the right place at all."

Meanwhile, Ian Pirie, from the local Friends of the Earth, is critical of the planning process so far, saying it has been "very undemocratic".

"They have not involved people," he says.

Demand for data centres is increasing, partly driven by AI needing more processing power.

At the moment, there are about 477 data centres across the UK and construction researchers Barbour ABI think that is going to increase by about 100.

Most of them will be in London and the South East.

The planning data suggests 28 of these new data centres will be within the Thames Water Catchment area, with 14 in Slough which already has the most data centres in Europe.

There are concerns about the amount of electricity and water data centres use.

A report for the Greater London Authority, London's Data Centre Future Growth Forecasts and Strategic Insights , outlines the challenges facing new data centres.

"Energy is the single most critical constraint on London's data centre growth," it says.

"Transmission grid capacity limitations have emerged particularly in west London, and new connection timelines for data centres may range from seven to 13 years, as compared to three to seven years in other European markets."

The report says water consumption is another "major consideration".

"A 100MW hyperscale data centre in the UK can consume up to 2.5 billion litres of water annually, equivalent to the needs of approximately 80,000 people, driving the shift toward closed-loop, air, and liquid immersion systems to reduce reliance on potable water," it says.

Data centres in London currently use about 5% of drinkable water, that is expected to rise to 7%.

The report also says: "High land costs and competition with housing and other industrial sectors make most plots in inner London and zone 2-3 challenging and may drive new development towards the edges of London."

It warns growth could put more strain on water systems.

The data centre industry is well established in London, but while it once prioritised security and secrecy, that is changing as operators become more open about why their services matter.

Mark Pestridge, chief executive of Telehouse, which operates data centres in London, says the centres underpin many of the services people rely on every day from streaming platforms to train timetables.

At the company's site in Canary Wharf, I asked how long would it take for people to notice if a data centre went down.

"I think they'd notice within minutes," he replied.

He says the industry needs to do more to explain its importance and there are "some myths we need to bust" around water and energy usage.

"In this building that we're in today, which is Telehouse South, we work on a closed loop system, which is a bit like your radiator or a fridge. The water just goes round and round, rather than ever taking water out of the system," he says.

"On electricity usage, I think we do use a lot of electricity, but I genuinely believe that the data centre is one of the most efficient as possible about how we use that electricity."

Some academics have urged caution over the pace of expansion.

Liz Stephens, professor of climate risks and resilience at the University of Reading, thinks the amount of extra water needed for data centres could potentially negate any extra capacity from new reservoirs.

"Thames Water had been trying to predict demand over the next 10 years," she says.

"They've estimated that about 30% of that increased demand is coming from the growth in data centres.

"And I think they've already admitted that they're underestimating the demand that's happened so far from those data centres."

But Matt Evans, from Tech UK, says the industry's environmental impact is often misunderstood.

"So data centres use a lot of energy, there's no getting around that, but the energy that they use is now nearly 100% carbon-free or renewable energy," he says.

"In terms of water, there's a lot of misunderstanding because a lot of that data comes from the United States which has a really different regulatory environment.

"Data centres in the UK use about 0.2% of our non-domestic, non-household water.

"So that's quite a small amount and the sector is determined to bring new technologies that are more efficient so that we use less water in new data centres going forward as well."

The draft London Plan, which guides councils on planning, says data centres in suitable locations should be supported in principle.

However, schemes should only be given the go-ahead if water and electricity capacity is available.

Sites allocated for housing should not be used and green belt land should only be considered if there are no brown field sites available.

"London is home to Europe's largest data centre cluster. They support the growth of important data-driven sectors and AI. But this growth will only deliver real benefits for London if the infrastructure that enables it is clean, efficient and aligned with the mayor's climate goals," it says.

The plan calls for facilities to be energy and water efficient, and to use innovative cooling technologies and, where possible, renewable energy sources. It also says data centres should be able to heat nearby homes through "heat recovery infrastructure".

London's mayor, Lord Sadiq Khan, says he wants London to have the most sustainable data centres in the world.

Digital Reef, the developer behind the North Ockendon scheme, was approached for comment but did not respond.

On its website, it says the project "will provide local employment opportunities and skills training" alongside new digital infrastructure and public green space.

The company says more than half the site would be dedicated to a 113-hectare ecology park - equivalent to more than 174 football pitches - with new footpaths and cycling routes.

Councillor Keith Prince, leader of Havering Council, says there will be further consultation on the scheme "when the time is right".

"Whilst we cannot prevent a private company from submitting a planning application, if the data centre were to go ahead, we will be driving the hardest bargain possible to maximise the benefits for Havering Residents and we would look to ensure there were ecological, environmental and agricultural gain," he adds.

No-one really knows how the predictions around data centres' water and electricity use will work out.

Could data centres become more efficient and use less? The data centre industry is moving from an era of secrecy and security to one of being more open.

It wants to emphasise how much of modern life is dependent on data centres - from reading this article to streaming the latest Netflix release.

Some argue we should lessen our dependence on these technologies, others say more data centres are the inevitable result of more AI use.

These huge buildings are crucial to much of modern life, but the dilemma is, at the moment, there seems to be little desire to welcome them into many communities.

articles.title: Artist Phil Lambert creates world's biggest soil painting
articles.summary: Phil Lambert used four types of soil, including some collected from his mother, to create his work.
articles.body:
An artist has set a record for the world's largest soil painting as he bids to raise awareness of how important the material is.

The UK-based Official Record Breakers has verified that organisation Save Soil had surpassed the previous best of 59,458 sq cm (about 64 sq ft), with the new painting measuring 61,000 sq cm (about 65 sq ft).

Phil Lambert, who lives in Cardiff, used four types of soil and an upcycled wooden frame and canvas supplied by Oxford Wood Recycling.

The artwork was created to raise awareness of the movement's call for soil regeneration to be prioritised at the 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP).

Save Soil is pushing for improvement of soil health around the world and works with governments to shape policies on the subject.

The painting, which Lambert created at University College London (UCL), follows its new report, which outlines the importance of healthy soils and steps for their restoration.

Lambert said he had been using soil for about 10 years and painting with it "is something I've been very familiar with".

As well as using soil from his garden and some from his mother's home, the artist also received donations from the James Hutton Institute in Scotland.

"I did have a motive in my mind of this tree and hedge and field," he said.

Through his work with scientists, Lambert said he had been taught about the "perils and the needs of soil".

"If you go back to the fields you were walking in when you were young, you will notice that there is a thinner soil on there and there's more rock on the surface," he said.

Listen to the latest news from Oxfordshire

UK Save Soil spokesperson Henry Asplin called the painting "a visual call to action".

"Soil is the planet's quiet infrastructure and one of our greatest climate solutions, yet it remains largely invisible in national climate plans," he said.

Mark Maslin, climate scientist and professor at UCL, said healthy soils "regulate water, store carbon, and underpin biodiversity and food systems".

"...protecting and restoring soil must sit at the heart of every nation's climate strategy if we are serious about limiting warming and securing a liveable future," he added.

Jennifer Robinson, from Abingdon-based Oxford Wood Recycling, said looking after the environment was "at the heart" of its work.

She said the company collected wood from several sites across Oxfordshire.

"I myself come from a farming background, so ... I think [Save Soil]'s cause and what they're trying to do is absolutely crucial," she said.

Robinson said she had been noticing changes in the colour of soil locally.

"We're all seeing massive cracks as we're out walking and the areas where there are more plants and more trees, the soil is less exposed and evidently healthier."

articles.title: Women in Luton hit poor health earlier than national average
articles.summary: Luton study reveals age of onset of poor health for women is five years below national average.
articles.body:
A study of female health in Luton has revealed that women in the town see the onset of poor health five years earlier than the national average.

The Let Women Speak report, commissioned by the Borough Council, also found over 70% of women aged 45-64 had an at-risk Body Mass Index (BMI) level.

Luton's director of public health Kelly O'Neill said: "Women are spinning a lot of plates as part of what the expectation of being a woman is, so many have put their own health and well-being secondary to the well-being of others.

"That meant they weren't turning up for cervical screening, breast screening and many things that help them stay healthier for longer."

More than 250 people from a range of ages and cultures were interviewed for the report that focuses on the wellbeing of the 112,400 women and girls who live in the town.

The study found the average age of onset of poor health for women in Luton is 55.8 years compared to 60.9 nationally. In June the BBC reported that life expectancy for women and men is also lower than the national average at 82.6 for women and 78.6 years for men.

24% of school-age girls in Luton skip breakfast and 15% skip lunch, which is often linked to stress, time pressure and concerns about body image.

Only 52.5% of women in Luton aged 25-49 take up cervical screening.

Only 27.3% of women in Luton access long-acting reversible contraception.

In 2025 only 63% of eligible women in Luton had a breast screening, compared to 71% nationally.

Councillors have now agreed to champion women's health and support the delivery of actions to improve health and wellbeing.

Dr Eva Patel is a GP at Luton Medical and Dental clinic. She said she often sees woman coming in who are managing multiple responsibilities.

"Working, bringing up children, looking after elderly parents or supporting other family members often from large families means their own physical and mental health is often the last thing they prioritise," she said.

Thirty-seven young South Asian women were also interviewed about their experience of social isolation.

Patel said: "Language can be a barrier. If a woman comes in by herself and they don't feel comfortable speaking English then they might find it difficult to explain symptoms, even with a translator."

articles.title: No strikes, no peace deal: How Trump plans to keep Iran under pressure
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump has settled on a third option in the Iran war, choosing to intensify economic pressure on Tehran rather than resume military
articles.body: US President Donald Trump has settled on a third option in the Iran war, choosing to intensify economic pressure on Tehran rather than resume military strikes or agree to a peace deal on terms Washington considers unacceptable, according to an Axios report.US secretary of state Marco Rubio outlined the administration's approach during a meeting with G7 foreign ministers on Tuesday, saying Trump was not limited to choosing between renewed military action and a negotiated agreement with Iran.Instead, Washington plans to continue its existing pressure campaign and further tighten the financial squeeze on Tehran, Axios reported."The President doesn't just have two options. It's not just returning to war or signing a ridiculous peace deal. We won't do a stupid deal. The third option we have is to continue to do what we do now," Rubio said.He argued that maintaining the current strategy would steadily increase the financial burden on Tehran without forcing Washington to set a deadline for ending the pressure campaign.The strategy aims to weaken Iran's financial infrastructure to the point where it struggles to fund armed groups or rebuild its military capabilities. Rubio also argued that Tehran was inflicting serious damage on its own economy by refusing to accept Washington's conditions."The President is not under false time pressure, the Iranians are inflicting major damage on their own economy," Rubio mentioned.The approach comes after months of uncertainty over the direction of the conflict. Trump has repeatedly threatened devastating military action against Iran while insisting that Tehran would eventually give in to Washington's demands. The conflict has also become a domestic political liability, with Republican candidates suffering setbacks in the midterm legislative contests.An American official close to the administration told Axios that Trump had been weighing several options without being certain which course to pursue. However, after meeting Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani on Monday, Trump signalled that he preferred to avoid another round of military strikes.He described the possibility of fresh attacks on Iranian targets as highly unlikely and unnecessary under the current circumstances.The administration instead plans to maintain its economic offensive and naval blockade while pursuing a new operation, 'Iron Gate'. The operation is aimed at dismantling ground transportation routes allegedly used to smuggle advanced weapons and technology.According to administration sources cited by Axios, Rubio was among the key figures in Trump's national security team who advocated this approach. Treasury secretary Scott Bessent, CIA director John Ratcliffe and presidential adviser Jared Kushner were also involved in the discussions.The officials reportedly opposed a renewed military escalation, arguing that Iran's current negotiating position remained fundamentally at odds with American interests. They favoured maintaining stringent financial pressure on the regime instead.Rubio also expressed doubts about the prospects of an immediate diplomatic breakthrough, saying Iran's preconditions for formal negotiations were unworkable. Speaking to reporters after the G7 ministerial meeting, he said Tehran wanted an agreement but had failed to put forward constructive proposals.He suggested that prolonged economic pressure would eventually force Iran to reconsider its position, as mounting financial difficulties would become increasingly difficult for its leadership to sustain."Eventually you have to eat," Rubio said, suggesting that basic material realities would eventually sway even the most uncompromising factions within the Iranian hierarchy.However, Washington's strategy of maintaining an extended economic squeeze has raised concerns among some of its key regional partners, including Turkey, Pakistan and Iraq, an administration official told Axios.The three countries reportedly have reservations about Washington's preference for indefinite financial pressure over efforts to secure a stable, negotiated settlement with Tehran.You use AI every day. articles.title: Jersey Electricity bills to rise by 2.5% from March
articles.summary: The increase will add just over £1 per week for a typical all-electric home, Jersey Electricity says.
articles.body:
Electricity bills will go up by 2.5% in Jersey from March 2027, it has been announced.

Jersey Electricity said the tariff increase would add just over £1 per week for a typical all-electric home from March 2027.

The annual rate of inflation in Jersey rose to 3% in September, according to the latest figures.

Chief executive Chris Ambler said: "We know that any increase in household costs is unwelcome, so we have worked hard to keep this rise below the island's current rate of inflation."

Ambler said: "We have again delayed the increase until March, which means it will not affect customers during the colder winter months when electricity consumption is generally at its highest."

The company said it was investing £120m in the network to improve its resilience and future-proof its systems.

It said it continued to focus on managing costs responsibly and driving efficiencies across the business.

articles.title: A different kind of drama - the actors creating pictures with sound
articles.summary: An audio drama workshop has brought blind and partially-sighted people together to create a new play.
articles.body:
A box of gravel, a handful of leaves and a miniature door might not sound like the ingredients for a wedding day drama.

But in a room filled with people experimenting with sounds, they are helping to bring an entire world to life.

For a group of blind and partially-sighted people, an audio-based drama workshop is giving them the chance to explore performance - without relying on visual cues.

Instead, they are using sound to create characters, settings and stories, building a picture in the audience's mind without showing them a single image.

The group is writing a play involving a jilted bride on her wedding day, alongside a household of well-meaning but chaotic characters.

Playing the bride, called Nuala with the Hula, Helen Kennedy never got the opportunity to do this in mainstream drama clubs.

"I love [amateur drama] but a lot of the clubs don't want me in the group because they're afraid I'll fall off the stage.

"Because my whole life is sightless and [this is] all sound based, this is just perfect for me."

Kennedy is one of a number of people taking part in the workshop, which is part of a two-year project by the organisation Sightless Cinema.

It creates cinema without pictures, with people who are blind and visually impaired using sound to tell stories and bring them to life.

The group experiment with props including a wind machine and a foley door - a miniature door with a latch used for sound effects - as well as different materials such as plastic and leaves.

"It's kind of tricky when you don't have any visual cues and you have to listen for your cue but it's really good fun," Kennedy says.

Another participant, Jim Masterson from Belfast, lost his sight after being assaulted when he was younger.

He has not taken part in drama since secondary school.

"It's good to get back into it again but it's different: Then I could see... now I'm completely blind."

Experimenting with sounds is something that Gareth Smyth has enjoyed.

"[Performing arts is] a way of expressing yourself... and I certainly feel that disabilities should not prevent you from doing so.

"It's not so much about the disability but it's about what the disability can enable you to do."

For Dorothy Leeman, the experience has also been an opportunity to discover what she can do.

She never imagined she could improvise the way she has - and has made new friends through the group.

"That was really, really good fun and I wouldn't have missed it for the world."

Andrew McBride loves the art of sound production and wanted to get involved.

He takes part in other dramatic performances and is used to performing in front of an audience - but improvising is "totally new" to him and "slightly terrifying".

Dawn Hopper says drama is in her blood and something she loved taking part in before experiencing significant sight loss.

She says Sightless Cinema is about "trying to paint a picture in people's minds" without the audience being able to see what is happening.

She adds it has been really educational to learn about the different tools and techniques.

Hopper says being involved in the arts can be difficult for those with sight loss because so much of it is visual.

"It's an opportunity to break down some of those barriers again.

"Just because you have sight loss, [it] doesn't mean that you can't be involved in arts."

Philip Chong wasn't sure what to expect at first - but thought it was going to be "a bit of craic [and] a bit of laughs at least".

For him, the experience has been "that and a lot more".

He says the workshop helped him to think on his feet and experience different types of drama.

The project will culminate in a performance in 2028, when audience members will be blindfolded in Queen's University Belfast's SARC Sonic Lab.

Ciarán Taylor, who runs the workshop, says it brings together theatre, sound and radio drama techniques - and gives people a reason to get out and meet each other.

"The greatest thing is the blind community and the sighted community getting together for these performances, which are a real celebration of creativity."

Sightless Cinema has also teamed up with Queen's University and the Royal National Institute of Blind People (RNIB), which helped recruit participants.

articles.title: A New Mexico woman posed as an IRS agent and convinced a victim to pay more than $150,000 in supposed fees to release a promised tax windfall; she has now pleaded guilty to five federal charges
articles.summary: A New Mexico woman impersonated an Internal Revenue Service (IRS) agent and convinced a victim that he would receive a large sum of money from the US tax
articles.body: A New Mexico woman impersonated an Internal Revenue Service (IRS) agent and convinced a victim that he would receive a large sum of money from the US tax agency if he first paid various fees and deposits. The victim handed over at least $150,000, believing the money would be transferred to the IRS, but the woman allegedly spent it on personal expenses. According to a November 9 announcement by the US Department of Justice (DOJ), Sandra Vega, 48, of Pecos, has now pleaded guilty to five federal charges in connection with the fraud scheme, which operated for nearly eight years.In her plea agreement, Vega admitted that she posed as an Internal Revenue agent between 2018 and March 2026 to defraud a man identified in court documents as John Doe. She persuaded him that he was entitled to receive a substantial payout from the IRS but needed to pay several fees and deposits before the money could be released.The victim made payments totalling at least $150,000, expecting that Vega would forward the amount to the federal tax agency. However, prosecutors said none of the money was ever sent to the IRS. Instead, Vega used the funds for her personal expenses.Five federal charges, faces up to 20 years in prisonVega pleaded guilty to four counts of wire fraud and one count of falsely impersonating a federal employee. The charges stem from her use of a fabricated government identity to persuade the victim to transfer money under false pretences. The case was announced by the US Attorney's Office for the District of New Mexico, along with officials from the IRS Criminal Investigation division and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI).At sentencing, Vega faces a maximum prison term of 20 years, a fine of up to $250,000 and an order to pay restitution to the victim. The amount of restitution will be determined by the court. However, Vega has not yet been sentenced, and the final punishment will be decided by the court.The investigation was conducted by the FBI's Albuquerque Field Office and IRS Criminal Investigation's Phoenix Field Office, with assistance from the Bernalillo County Sheriff's Office and the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration. The US Attorney's Office for the District of New Mexico is prosecuting the case.IRS warns against impersonation and fake refund schemesThe IRS has repeatedly warned taxpayers about scammers who impersonate its employees through phone calls, emails, text messages and social media. Such fraudsters may claim that a person is entitled to a refund, tax credit or government payment, or threaten legal consequences unless money is transferred immediately.According to the IRS, unexpected communications promising unusually large refunds or demanding immediate payments should be treated with caution. The agency advises taxpayers to independently verify suspicious communications rather than relying on phone numbers, links or contact details provided by the person approaching them. The IRS also says it generally initiates contact with taxpayers through letters or notices delivered by the US Postal Service. It does not send unsolicited social media direct messages or demand immediate payment through gift cards.In a separate warning about tax-related scams, the agency has highlighted how fraudsters exploit the possibility of receiving large refunds or credits to convince people to share personal and financial information or pay upfront fees. The US government's consumer protection guidance similarly warns that impersonation scams often involve individuals claiming to represent official agencies, businesses or other trusted organisations. Their objective is to gain a victim's confidence before requesting money or sensitive information.How taxpayers can identify suspicious IRS communicationsThe IRS recommends checking whether a communication is genuine before responding to requests for money or personal information. Taxpayers who receive suspicious calls can hang up and contact the agency through its official website or verified telephone numbers. The agency also advises people not to click on suspicious links or share sensitive financial information in response to unexpected messages claiming to offer refunds or tax benefits.Vega's case involved a victim who continued making payments over several years in the expectation of receiving a large government payout. With her guilty plea, the case now moves towards sentencing, where the court will determine the prison term, financial penalty and restitution owed to the victim.You use AI every day. articles.title: Headquarters of Haitian gang destroyed, El Salvador's president says
articles.summary: The infamous 400 Mawozo gang was targeted by the El Salvador military which has deployed thousands of troops to combat Haiti's gang violence crisis.
articles.body:
The headquarters of one of Haiti's largest crime gangs has been destroyed by El Salvador's military, the Salvadoran president has said.

The infamous 400 Mawozo gang, which is known for kidnappings and intimidation tactics, was targeted in a ground and air attack at a complex on the outskirts of Haiti's capital, Port-au-Prince.

It is El Salvador's first military action on a Haitian target since it deployed more than 2,000 soldiers there last month, as part of a mission to rescue four missing Salvadoran technicians.

Haiti has been plagued by gang violence for years, with heavily armed groups controlling large parts of the capital, and beyond.

El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele announced the news on X , boasting that most of the gang members fled without trying to fight.

"We destroyed the house of [gang leader] Lanmò San Jou and the 400 Mawozo gang's headquarters," he wrote on Tuesday.

The post was accompanied by video of several helicopters firing on a large complex, reportedly in the suburb of Croix-des-Bouquets, the gang's stronghold.

As the helicopters circle above, dozens of people can be seen running out of the property, fleeing the strikes.

Several media outlets have reported that as many as 20 people were killed, however that has not been confirmed by authorities. There has also been no official confirmation of the extent of the damage at the property, with Haitians questioning whether it has been destroyed or just damaged.

The Miami Herald reports that the gang's leader, Wilson "Lanmò San Jou" Joseph, was not there at the time.

The BBC has not been able to verify the video posted by Bukele, nor whether the property is indeed the gang's headquarters.

Haiti's National Police drone task force was involved in the attack, supported by Salvadoran soldiers, the Miami Herald reports, citing several sources.

Posting on X after the strikes, Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé thanked the Salvadoran military's commitment "in the fight against gangs", and said the two nations would keep working together, along with the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), to "regain control of the territory and restore state authority".

"THE GANGS WILL GET NO SLEEP!" he added.

Some 2,000 Salvadoran soldiers were deployed to Haiti last month after four air force technicians were abducted at gunpoint while food shopping in October.

El Salvador's right-wing president has vowed to bring the men home alive and warned the gang to release them immediately or face sustained pressure from his military.

The four abducted men were working as part of the GSF, made up of troops from several nations, initially led by soldiers from Chad.

President Bukele's move to send thousands of Salvadoran troops to Haiti has raised concerns, with critics saying they are not all working within the command structure of the GSF. It has raised questions about the operational legitimacy and legality of their actions in the Caribbean nation.

Amnesty International has urged both countries to "ensure all operations conducted by Salvadoran forces in Haiti comply with international human rights law".

Such concerns do not appear to faze Bukele, however, who continues to directly warn and target the gang leaders.

The attack on the supposed gang headquarters seemingly came after a user on X had urged Bukele to attack the complex.

"Where is that house? Give us the exact address, and we'll destroy it," he replied to the post, which has now been taken down, apparently for violating X's rules.

The 400 Mawozo gang is the largest criminal organisation in Haiti, and known for kidnappings, extortion, murders and arms trafficking.

Haiti is the poorest country in the Americas and remains largely under gang control.

At least 5,700 people have been killed or injured there by gangs or during operations against them between 1 January and 11 September this year alone, the United Nations has said.

El Salvador has recorded huge reductions in gang violence under President Bukele as part of a sweeping crackdown, and he has vowed to do the same in Haiti.

However, human rights groups have argued that the way he has done it is unlawful, with the open-ended extension of emergency laws, the treatment of detainees in El Salvador's high-security mega-prison and the mass trials of alleged gang members.

articles.title: Microsoft sends 'China ban warning' to the US government; says: Datacenters across America will come to a grinding halt if you …
articles.summary: Microsoft has sent a ‘warning’ to the White House saying that data centres in the US will come to a halt if the FCC’s proposed import ban on Chinese
articles.body: Microsoft has sent a ‘warning’ to the White House saying that data centres in the US will come to a halt if the FCC’s proposed import ban on Chinese optical transceivers is passed. According to a Reuters report, the software giant is lobbying against the move alongside the Information Technology Industry Council (ITI). Microsoft, which is building 35 data centers around the country and is planning 134 more, reportedly met the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy and the National Security Council recently.“It really threatens to arguably grind (the data center rollout) to a halt,” ITI Executive Vice President of Policy and General Counsel John Miller said. “Those chips, without optical transceivers, literally could just sit there waiting around unutilized until you actually have the transceivers to essentially connect them together,” he further stated referring to the AI chips that data centers use.What are optical transceivers that FCC wants to ban import from ChinaOptical transceivers are small devices that convert electrical signals into light signals, allowing data to travel through fibre-optic cables. Data centres increasingly use this technology to transfer data between AI chips and server racks. Compared with traditional copper cables, fibre-optic connections are faster, have lower delays, use less power and produce less heat.However, Chinese companies account for 66% of the global optical transceiver market. A ban on these companies supplying US data centres is expected to cut the available supply by more than half, worsening the shortages already affecting the industry.Concerns against China-made optical transceiversAs stated in a Tom’s Hardware report, there are concerns that some of the optical transceivers could be compromised by Beijing which in turn can be used to steal data, install malware, or remotely disrupt American data centers. This is the likely reason why FCC is considering the ban.Notably, only two US-based companies – Coherent and Lumentum produce optical transceivers that data centers need. However, the firms don’t have the scale to make up for the shortfall if the FCC bans Chinese imports.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: On Christmas Eve 1971, 17-year-old Juliane Koepcke fell about 3,000 metres, still strapped to her seat, from LANSA Flight 508, which was struck by lightning over Peru;  the only survivor of the 92 people on board, she walked through the Amazon rainforest for 11 days
articles.summary: Juliane Koepcke, 71, has never struggled to recount the Christmas of 1971. She was just 17, flying home to see her father in Panguana.
articles.body: Juliane Koepcke, 71, has never struggled to recount the Christmas of 1971. She was just 17, flying home to see her father in Panguana. The passengers were already frustrated after a seven-hour delay when the aircraft encountered a violent thunderstorm over the Peruvian rainforest. Fear glistened in her eyes as she saw the lightning around the plane. Scared, she held her mother’s hand tightly. Neither of them could speak. The other passengers began to scream and weep.“After about 10 minutes, I saw a very bright light on the outer engine on the left. My mother said very calmly, ‘That is the end, it's all over.’ Those were the last words I ever heard from her,” Koepcke recounted to the BBC, 40 years after the incident.The plane went into a nosedive, and all she could see was pitch black and the people screaming. The engine’s roar drowned out all other noises. Then the noise stopped, and she was out in the sky, in a free fall, still strapped to her seat. Juliane plunged thousands of metres towards the jungle as LANSA Flight 508 broke apart in mid-air. The last thing she could remember was the whispering of the wind. She felt completely alone. Then nothing. She lost consciousness. She woke up the next day, all alone, and all she could think was, “I survived an air crash.” For the next 10 days, she wandered through the rainforest before being rescued on the eleventh day. She was the only one of the 92 people aboard to walk out of the jungle alive.Waking up in the jungleWhen she woke the next morning, Koepcke called out desperately for her mother, but there was no response. She was completely alone. Recalling the moments before the crash, she remembered that her mother had grown anxious as the plane entered the heavy clouds. The violent turbulence that followed had made her even more nervous.Before she could gather her thoughts, Koepcke became aware of her injuries. She had a broken collarbone and deep cuts on her legs. She had also lost her glasses and one of her sandals, and she was wearing a sleeveless mini-dress. She had a ruptured ligament in her knee. “My injuries weren't serious, so I could still walk.”Wandering in the rainforest for 10 daysBorn to German parents in 1954, Juliane Koepcke was raised in the Peruvian jungle, ABC reported. Her father, Hans-Wilhelm Koepcke, was a renowned zoologist, and her mother, Maria Koepcke, was a scientist who studied tropical birds. They had a biological research station called Panguana in the rainforest. Having grown up on the station as a 'jungle child', she knew how to survive.“Before the crash, I had spent a year and a half with my parents at their research station, only 30 miles away. I learned a lot about life in the rainforest, and that it wasn't too dangerous. It's not the green hell that the world always thinks,” she told the British broadcaster.She knew she had to survive alone. So she found a creek and stuck to the water. The only food she had was a bag of sweets from the wreckage, and they didn’t last. She knew the things she had to avoid: snakes camouflaged as dry leaves and the changing weather. She also heard planes overhead searching for the wreckage. But unfortunately, they couldn’t see her through the dense canopy.On the fourth day, she heard a king vulture land nearby. She knew they came down only for carrion. Around a bend in the water, she found a bench seat with three passengers jammed headfirst into the mud. It was her first time seeing a corpse. As a 17-year-old, it wasn’t easy for her. Her first thought was that one of them was her mother. “But when I touched the corpse with a stick, I saw that the woman's toenails were painted. My mother never polished her nails. I was immediately relieved but then felt ashamed of that thought,” she told the broadcaster.Day 10: Maggots appeared in her wound\By the tenth day, she could barely stand. She drifted along a larger river until she saw what looked like a big boat, and she thought she was hallucinating. But it was real. Up a small path, she found a hut with a palm-leaf roof, an outboard motor and a litre of petrol.By then, the wound on her upper right arm was infested with maggots. It was about one centimetre long. That was when her childhood memories came to her aid. “I remembered our dog had the same infection, and my father had put kerosene in it, so I sucked the petrol out and put it into the wound. The pain was intense as the maggots tried to get further into the wound. I pulled out about 30 maggots and was very proud of myself.”She spent the night there. The next morning, she heard men’s voices outside. “It was like hearing the voices of angels,” she recalled. When they saw her, they froze. They took her for a water goddess from local legend. She spoke to them in Spanish, explained what had happened, and they took her back to civilisation.Ninety-two people were on the plane: 86 passengers and six crew members, according to the Aviation Safety Network. Ninety-one died. Up to 14 of those who survived the impact died while waiting for rescue, and Juliane’s mother was among them. Juliane was the only one found alive who was able to walk out of the jungle.The day after the rescue, she was reunited with her father. He could barely speak. Searchers recovered her mother’s body on 12 January. She later learned that her mother had also survived the initial crash but was so badly injured that she died several days later. Now 71, Koepcke is a biologist. She sees the world just as her parents did. And every detail of Christmas Eve 1971 remains vivid.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: After 47 years of marriage, a Missouri couple split a joint trust worth nearly $895,000; when the husband died, his wife challenged a promise involving his $505,000 IRA, and a court upheld a medical trust
articles.summary: A Missouri couple who had been married for 47 years divided their nearly $895,000 joint trust equally in September 2021, after the husband promised that
articles.body: A Missouri couple who had been married for 47 years divided their nearly $895,000 joint trust equally in September 2021, after the husband promised that his separate $505,000 retirement account would cover his wife's extraordinary medical expenses if he died first. But when he was killed in a car accident barely two months later, the widow discovered that she was not named as a beneficiary of the account. A subsequent legal battle over the unwritten promise reached the Missouri Court of Appeals, which on November 10, 2026, upheld a court-created medical trust funded with $505,000 from the husband's estate. In its ruling in 'In the Matter of Ray Bergfeld, Deceased' (ED113884), the Missouri Court of Appeals affirmed the lower court's decision to protect Mary Alice Bergfeld's access to money for major and traumatic medical expenses, while rejecting her request for broader access to the retirement funds.Couple divided nearly $895,000 joint trustMary Alice and Ray "Buzz" Bergfeld had been married for 47 years and had children from previous marriages. They maintained separate individual retirement accounts (IRAs) and revocable living trusts to ensure their respective estates would eventually pass to their own children. However, they also established a joint trust in 2006 to provide financial security for both spouses during their lifetimes. By September 1, 2021, the trust held $894,638.75 in a Morgan Stanley account.Buzz wanted to divide the money so he could pass his share to his children while he was still alive. He initially proposed that he receive 60% and Mary Alice 40%, but she rejected the arrangement. After several rounds of negotiations, he eventually offered an equal division.As part of the agreement, Buzz told his wife that if he died first, his son Bob would manage his approximately $505,000 IRA and use it to pay for her extraordinary medical expenses. Any money left in the account after her death would go to his children.Mary Alice agreed to the 50:50 division. On or around September 10, 2021, the couple withdrew the assets from the joint account, divided them and terminated the trust.Husband died before IRA arrangement was implementedUnknown to Mary Alice, Buzz had begun consulting an attorney in April 2021 about dividing the joint trust. His financial adviser had referred him to the lawyer, and some of Buzz's children attended meetings. The judgment noted that Buzz asked his attorney to send legal bills to his daughter Mona's home rather than the marital residence so that Mary Alice would not know he had hired legal counsel. He also took his wife's individual estate-planning documents from a safety deposit box without her knowledge and gave them to his attorney.His lawyer reportedly suggested preparing a postnuptial agreement to document the arrangement, but Buzz instructed him not to proceed because he believed Mary Alice would not accept its terms.On November 22, 2021, Buzz died in a car accident. When Mary Alice subsequently asked his son Bob about the IRA, she was told she was not listed as its beneficiary. She later filed a lawsuit against her husband's estate, alleging fraudulent and negligent misrepresentation over the promise concerning the retirement account.Court limits access to major medical expensesIn May 2025, the trial court ruled that Buzz had negligently misrepresented the arrangement because he failed to exercise reasonable care in making the promise without putting a plan in place to fulfil it. However, it did not find sufficient evidence that he knowingly made a false promise, which was necessary to establish fraud.The court created an equitable trust funded with $505,000 from Buzz's estate. It restricted the money to major and traumatic medical expenses, including hospital treatment, prescription medicines, rehabilitation, medically necessary equipment and long-term care. Mary Alice appealed, arguing that the money should also cover her general support and that the trust should have taken effect from the date of Buzz's death rather than the 2025 judgment.The appellate court rejected both arguments. It noted that Mary Alice's own income and assets were sufficient to meet her living expenses, even after several hospitalisations and her move to assisted living. At the time of trial, she was 91 years old, earned approximately $100,000 annually and had assets exceeding $1.5 million.The court also rejected her claim of fraudulent misrepresentation, noting that testimony from her daughter supported the finding that Buzz had promised to speak to his son about managing the IRA in the future, rather than claiming that he had already done so.The estate also challenged the negligent misrepresentation finding, arguing that the couple's private financial discussions did not constitute a business transaction. However, the appellate court held that the management and division of their joint trust, involving financial advisers and legal professionals, qualified as a transaction in which Buzz had a financial interest.The Missouri Court of Appeals ultimately affirmed the lower court's judgment, preserving the $505,000 medical trust for Mary Alice while ensuring that any remaining funds after her death would pass to Buzz's children.You use AI every day. articles.title: Successive governments asleep at the wheel on social care, says head of review
articles.summary: Baroness Casey criticises variability of services and fees charged to self-funders in England.
articles.body:
Successive governments have been "asleep at the wheel" on adult social care, says the head of the independent commission looking into the sector in England.

Baroness Louise Casey said care services for older people and adults with disabilities had been developed in a largely uncontrolled and unintended way, unlike the deliberate design of the NHS in 1948.

As a result, she suggested a postcode lottery had developed with different levels of services available depending on where people live.

And she also highlighted the fees that self-funders pay, saying they were much higher than councils were charged for people entitled to state support.

Baroness Casey said care services were simply not valued enough.

Speaking to the Today programme on Radio 4, she said the NHS had become a "national hospital service: that was focussed on medical care".

And she said the failings identified by the recent Covid inquiry report into social care were testament to that.

Last month the inquiry published a report which said the care sector appeared to be " something of an afterthought" in the early stages of the pandemic, allowing Covid to spread like "wildfire" .

Baroness Casey, who will address a conference of social care leaders later on Wednesday, said the findings were "so awful" and "a national shame".

"Successive governments have been asleep at the wheel. We've got our heads in the sand."

Her final recommendations for services for older people and adults with disabilities will be published next summer.

It comes as her commission publishes research showing England is an international outlier for having no "clear system of stewardship" for social care, unlike countries such as France and Germany.

She said the market was dominated by private providers and said the regulator – the Care Quality Commission – as being a "spectator at the site of a car crash".

Two people with the same condition having different experiences depending on where they live – different assement processes, waits and levels of support

Those who paid for their own care – social care is means-tested – are charged on average 40% more than the councils pay for care they arrange

When Andy Burnham became prime minister, he said social care was one of his key priorities although the Casey commission was set up by the Starmer government.

"Together, we can build a new settlement for care," Baroness Casey said.

"One based on values I still believe this country shares – decency, contribution and a duty to care for our neighbours, our loved ones and ourselves."
